item.title: Unconventional DNA architecture in a dopamine–bound aptamer complex
item.dc:creator: Emily Hoi Pui Chao
Eric Largy
Yunus A. Kaiyum
Minh-Dat Nguyen
Brune Vialet
Philippe Dauphin-Ducharme
Philip E. Johnson
Cameron D. Mackereth
item.description:
Authors: Emily Hoi Pui Chao, Eric Largy, Yunus A. Kaiyum, Minh-Dat Nguyen, Brune Vialet, Philippe Dauphin-Ducharme, Philip E. Johnson, Cameron D. Mackereth
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Aptamers are oligonucleotides that have been selected to bind a particular target. Despite the growing popularity of functional DNA aptamers, there remains limited knowledge of their binding mechanisms, as few have been characterized at the atomic level. Here, we use NMR spectroscopy to obtain structural details of RKEC1, a shortened version of a DNA aptamer previously reported to bind dopamine. We find that RKEC1 forms a compact structure upon ligand binding that lacks any Watson-Crick duplex regions or G-quadruplex core, in stark contrast to nearly all predicted and observed DNA aptamer folds. The atomic details explain dopamine specificity amongst structurally similar compounds, and the determined DNA fold was used to guide biosensor design. The aptamer structure further suggests that DNA folding can access an extensive conformational landscape reminiscent of RNA, thus expanding the diversity traditionally captured by predictive algorithms.

item.title: The extracellular turret as a structural hub for voltage sensor-pore coupling in HCN channels
item.dc:creator: Kaei Ryu
Go Kasuya
Koichi Nakajo
item.description:
Authors: Kaei Ryu, Go Kasuya, Koichi Nakajo
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels are essential for rhythmic electrical activity in cardiac and neuronal cells, and their dysfunction underlies disorders such as arrhythmia and epilepsy. Although HCN channels share a conserved six-transmembrane architecture with voltage-gated K⁺ (Kv) channels, how voltage-sensing domains (VSDs) are coupled to pore opening remains incompletely understood. Here, we identify an extracellular pathway that couples voltage-sensor movement to pore opening via the extracellular turret helix, which acts as a critical determinant of voltage-dependent gating in HCN channels. Alanine-scanning mutagenesis of HCN4 revealed six turret residues whose substitution abolished hyperpolarization-evoked currents. Voltage-clamp fluorometry showed that these mutations preserved S4 activation while selectively disrupting turret conformational changes, thereby uncoupling VSD movement from pore opening. Structural and functional analyses further identified an extracellular interaction network linking the turret to the S1, S5, and S6 segments that is essential for hyperpolarization-dependent gating. Collectively, these findings identify the extracellular turret as an active gating hub that coordinates concerted extracellular rearrangements to transmit voltage-sensor displacement to the pore. On the basis of these results, we propose a hand-in-hand coupling model, in which turret rearrangements act as a key downstream relay in the voltage-dependent opening of HCN channels.

item.title: Predicting protein electrostatics with protein language models
item.dc:creator: Mingzhe Shen
Guy W. Dayhoff II
Daniel Kortzak
Jana Shen
item.description:
Authors: Mingzhe Shen, Guy W. Dayhoff II, Daniel Kortzak, Jana Shen
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Ionization states are crucial to protein function, yet predicting their equilibrium constants remains challenging. Here we present KaML-ESMs, sequence-based neural networks built on the ESM protein language models and trained on the GAINES-augmented PKAD-3r dataset. KaML-ESM2/ESMC outperform alternative approaches across four benchmarks, achieving root-mean-square errors of about 0.5 units for Asp/Glu/His/Cys/Tyr/Lys residues in native proteins. Performance degrades on 89 buried engineered mutations lacking evolutionary support, revealing a limitation that supervised training may help overcome. These results suggest that protein sequence, through its evolutionary context, encodes not only structure and function but also, indirectly, electrostatic characteristics. Applying KaML-ESM2 to the entire human proteome, we show that predicted p K a values can identify functional sites and infer catalytic mechanisms. We offer KaML, a sequence-based p K a prediction platform supporting biological exploration, protein engineering, and biomolecular simulation. With further development, GAINES could provide a general framework for addressing data scarcity in machine learning.

item.title: Education-related polygenic scores show different associations with youth mental health in parent-offspring trios
item.dc:creator: José J. Morosoli
Elizabeth Orpwood
Tim T. Morris
Abigail R. ter Kuile
Andrea G. Allegrini
Jean-Baptiste Pingault
item.description:
Authors: José J. Morosoli, Elizabeth Orpwood, Tim T. Morris, Abigail R. ter Kuile, Andrea G. Allegrini, Jean-Baptiste Pingault
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Educational attainment and mental health are associated from childhood, but less is known about how this association is reflected within families, where children’s genetic variation is correlated with both parental genotypes and family environments. We examine whether associations involving children’s own and parental polygenic scores differ for cognitive and non-cognitive genetic components of educational attainment. These scores aggregate common DNA variants using weights from genome-wide association studies. We analyse 3,223 mother-father-child trios from the UK Millennium Cohort Study using structural equation models that jointly estimate associations involving children’s own and parental polygenic scores. Here we show that cognitive and non-cognitive education-related polygenic scores are associated with externalising behaviour, including hyperactivity and conduct problems, and internalising behaviour, including anxiety and low mood, across childhood and adolescence. Associations are generally larger in magnitude for externalising than internalising behaviour, with clearer component-specific differences for externalising behaviour. These findings highlight the heterogeneity in education-related polygenic score associations with youth mental health within families.

item.title: Phylogenomics of captured Cryptosporidium sequenced directly from patient samples identifies clade-specific genomic architecture and host-adapted lineages
item.dc:creator: E. V. C. Alves-Ferreira
A. Khan
M. D. Tettey
F. Ihara
H. Vogel
S. Botchie
I. Ayi
M. C. Pawlowic
item.description:
Authors: E. V. C. Alves-Ferreira, A. Khan, M. D. Tettey, F. Ihara, H. Vogel, S. Botchie, I. Ayi, M. C. Pawlowic, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Cryptosporidium causes diarrhea and high mortality in young children in Africa and southern Asia. Low oocyst counts in stool often limit whole-genome sequencing from clinical samples. Here, we enrich for Cryptosporidium genomic DNA directly from stool samples using 74,973 RNA baits (CryptoCap_75K; 8.2 Mb) derived from gene-rich areas (100% coding capacity) within the Cryptosporidium parvum genome. This method produces genome-wide sequence data with sufficient depth and breadth of coverage using as few as 25 oocysts, including divergent species such as Cryptosporidium ubiquitum . To minimize reference bias, we utilize a dual-mapping strategy that integrates reads aligned to both C. parvum and C. ubiquitum to capture lineage-specific variation. Phylogenetic networks, haplotypes, and admixture analyses identify three C. ubiquitum groups, A and B exclusive to humans, with B showing evidence of admixture, whereas C is zoonotic. Group-specific polymorphisms cluster within discrete genomic regions, suggesting conserved haploblocks associate with host adaptation. This capture-based genomics approach provides high-resolution insights into Cryptosporidium population genetics and lays the groundwork for studies of zoonotic transmission, anthroponosis, and GWAS directly from clinical material.

item.title: Extracorporeal photopheresis for the treatment of steroid-refractory immune related adverse events from immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy: a multi-center phase Ib/II clinical trial
item.dc:creator: Roxane Riemer
Lukas M. Braun
Sophie Giesler
David Rafei-Shamsabadi
Sebastian Haferkamp
Alina Hartmann
Wolfgang Melchinger
Matthias Weiss
item.description:
Authors: Roxane Riemer, Lukas M. Braun, Sophie Giesler, David Rafei-Shamsabadi, Sebastian Haferkamp, Alina Hartmann, Wolfgang Melchinger, Matthias Weiss, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11078
Abstract: Abstract Severe immune-related adverse events (irAE) in cancer patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) require treatment interruption and immunosuppression. Based on prior preclinical data, in this prospective, single arm, non-randomized phase-Ib/II clinical trial we test the activity of Extracorporeal Photopheresis (ECP) against steroid-refractory irAEs in 30 patients (EudraCT-No.:2021-002073-26). The primary endpoint is the evaluation of the safety of ECP treatment for patients with ICI-induced irAEs. The study meets its pre-specified primary endpoint of less than 50% of patients developing ECP-related severe adverse events (SAE). No ECP-related SAE is observed and ECP-related AEs are reported in 20% (6/30) of patients. Overall response rate for all irAEs is 96.3% (CI 81.0–99.91). Colitis-, hepatitis- and dermatitis-specific response rates are 100% (13/13), 86.7% (13/15) and 100% (3/3), respectively. Secondary endpoints include the assessment of response rate of irAE and overall survival. ECP therapy is associated with reduced granzyme-A/B/K, T-bet, interferon-γ and TNF in peripheral T cells and pro-inflammatory gene-expression in the intestinal tract. The 12-month overall survival rate is 84.3% (CI 63.4%-93.8%). Response correlates with a decrease in inflammatory gene expression in the intestinal tract. These results suggest that ECP is a safe treatment option for SR-irAEs and warrant further investigation in subsequent randomized clinical trials.

item.title: Tyramine mediates radiation-induced bystander effects
item.dc:creator: Zirui Huang
Jiane-Kang Liu
Wenyuan He
Longnong You
Lizhu Zhang
Yongsheng Chen
Yaoyong Zeng
Yuxin Guo
item.description:
Authors: Zirui Huang, Jiane-Kang Liu, Wenyuan He, Longnong You, Lizhu Zhang, Yongsheng Chen, Yaoyong Zeng, Yuxin Guo, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Radiation-induced bystander effects (RIBEs) compromise radioprotection and radiotherapy by propagating damage to non-irradiated cells; however, the mediators and underlying circuitry remain incompletely defined. Using localised UV irradiation as the primary experimental system and localised X-ray irradiation as a supportive test in an in vivo Caenorhabditis elegans model, we identify tyramine, a trace amine structurally and functionally related to adrenaline/noradrenaline, as a neuron-derived mediator of RIBEs. Tyramine released from tyraminergic RIM neurons activates TYRA-3, a tyramine-responsive adrenergic-like GPCR related to vertebrate adrenergic receptors. This neuron-to-intestine signal promotes secretion of the insulin-like peptide INS-5, aberrantly engages the DAF-2/insulin signalling pathway (IIS), and triggers endoplasmic reticulum stress, DNA damage responses, and embryonic lethality in non-irradiated tissues. These findings reveal a neuro–intestinal–germline axis that orchestrates RIBEs and uncover an unanticipated role for adrenaline-like signalling. Our work provides a conceptual framework for systematically discovering additional RIBE mediators and identifies pathway components for future evaluation as radioprotective or radiotherapy-modifying targets.

item.title: Multi-omics profiling of primary human B cells activated via distinct stimuli
item.dc:creator: Vitor R. C. Aguiar
Marcella E. Franco
Nada Abdel Aziz
Daniela Fernandez-Salinas
Marcos Chiñas
Mariasilvia Colantuoni

item.description:
Authors: Vitor R. C. Aguiar, Marcella E. Franco, Nada Abdel Aziz, Daniela Fernandez-Salinas, Marcos Chiñas, Mariasilvia Colantuoni, Qian Xiao, Nicolaj Hackert, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract B cells are central for immunity and immune-mediated diseases (IMD), but how distinct signaling pathways drive diverse activation responses over time is not comprehensively understood. Here, we obtain peripheral blood B cells from 27 female healthy donors for in vitro stimulation, profiling the response at multiple time points using RNA-seq, single-cell RNA-seq with surface protein markers (CITE-seq), and ATAC-seq. Using diverse stimuli including activation of the B cell receptor (BCR), Toll-like receptor 7 (TLR7), TLR9, CD40, and differentiation into double negative 2 (DN2) IgD – CD27 – CD11c + CD21 – B cells, our analyses uncover activation-dependent B cell states, stimulation-specific transcription factors and regulatory regions, the dynamic response of IMD-associated gene expression, and specific open chromatin regions associated with IMD genetic risk. Furthermore, we also identify a lupus risk variant in an enhancer regulating TNFSF4 expression. The analysis data can be accessed via an interactive browser: https://mgalab.shinyapps.io/bcellactivation . Our findings underscore how profiling the full breadth of B cell activation pathways may be important for understanding B cell biology in health and disease.

item.title: Suppressor tRNAs restore functionally enhanced tumour suppressor protein to induce tumour regression
item.dc:creator: Bangyan Kong
Zhetao Zheng
Zeyuan Mi
Zhiyang Dou
Yuelin Yang
Yuxuan Shen
Liangzhen Dong
Jingru Lv
item.description:
Authors: Bangyan Kong, Zhetao Zheng, Zeyuan Mi, Zhiyang Dou, Yuelin Yang, Yuxuan Shen, Liangzhen Dong, Jingru Lv, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Nonsense mutations in tumour suppressor genes (TSGs) drive cancer initiation and progression but remain “undruggable” due to formidable challenges in rescuing the functional impairment of heterogeneous truncated proteins with a single agent. Here we observe that suppressor transfer RNAs (sup-tRNAs) can overcome diverse nonsense mutations in TP53 , restoring full-length p53 expression and function. Sup-tRNAs enable high-fidelity incorporation of optimal amino acids and can further enhance the transcriptional activity of p53 to suppress tumour cell proliferation. Moreover, we employ a computational model to guide sup-tRNA design by in silico saturation mutagenesis for targeted readthrough of different nonsense-mutant TSGs. Remarkably, sup-tRNAs produced p53 variants with enhanced activity relative to restored wild-type p53, reducing cancer cell colony area by up to 82%. In two xenograft models harbouring nonsense mutant TP53 , we observed up to a 74% reduction in tumour volume after lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-based sup-tRNA treatment, attributed to robust recovery of p53 expression and function. Critically, sup-tRNA monotherapy surpassed nab-paclitaxel chemotherapy in efficacy, and their combination induced near-complete tumour regression (a maximum of 93% reduction in tumour volume) without detectable toxicity in multiple mouse tumour models. Our findings highlight the potential of tRNA-based therapy to provide a promising strategy for rescuing nonsense-mutant TP53 .

item.title: Cosmogenic isotopic evidence from Chang’e-6 clasts for excavation history and ejecta provenance in the South Pole-Aitken basin
item.dc:creator: Mi Zhou
Yingnan Zhang
Jian Chen
Ruixuan Luo
Ziwei Wang
Zhiwei Zuo
Deliang Chen
Kewei Chen
item.description:
Authors: Mi Zhou, Yingnan Zhang, Jian Chen, Ruixuan Luo, Ziwei Wang, Zhiwei Zuo, Deliang Chen, Kewei Chen, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Impact and space weathering play a key role in resurfacing the Moon, yet their effects on the lunar farside remain poorly constrained. Chang’e-6 (CE-6) samples provide a unique opportunity to understand space weathering and material redistributions within the South Pole-Aitken (SPA) Basin. Our combined cosmogenic Sm, Hf, and Cr isotope results indicate an average cosmic-ray exposure (CRE) age of ~500 Ma for the CE-6 soil. Most low-Ti basaltic clasts experienced prolonged exposure similar to the host soil, whereas two were excavated more recently. Three KREEP-bearing clasts falling into two compositional groups show non-overlapping CRE ages, indicative of different excavation histories. Comparison with remote-sensing data suggests the Mg-rich pyroxene annulus and cryptomare as candidate source regions, respectively. These findings suggest that KREEP components are more widely distributed across the lunar farside than previously recognized.

item.title: Prefrontal cortex and striatum dissociate modality and learning order in cross-modal sensorimotor learning in mice
item.dc:creator: Da Song
Andrew J. Peters
item.description:
Authors: Da Song, Andrew J. Peters
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Sensorimotor learning is accompanied by the emergence of sensory responses in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) and striatum. However, it remains unclear whether these learning-evoked sensory regions are modality-specific, or whether they represent a more generalized signal for behaviorally relevant stimuli. We addressed this question by recording activity in the cortex and striatum of mice during training on visual and auditory sensorimotor tasks. We found that the anterior PFC developed context-dependent responses to both stimulus modalities after learning, while the medial PFC developed context-independent visual responses. Mice were able to transfer learned behavior from visual to auditory stimuli, but not the reverse. The training order of modalities did not affect responses in the PFC, while transferring from visual to auditory modalities drove auditory responses in a visually responsive region of the striatum. These findings reveal that learned sensory responses in the PFC and striatum uniquely dissociate modality and learning order.

item.dc:creator: Cameron N. Deakin
Iulia Turcas
Benjamin L. L. Réant

Adam Brookfield

item.description:
Authors: Cameron N. Deakin, Iulia Turcas, Benjamin L. L. Réant, Liam P. Griffin, John A. Seed, Adam Brookfield, David Collison, Eric J. L. McInnes, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10914
Abstract: Abstract Uranocene, [U IV (η 8 -C 8 H 8 ) 2 ], is the actinide equivalent to ferrocene. While ferrocene is readily oxidised to the ferrocenium cation, higher oxidation states of uranocene are unknown. Here we report the elusive uranocenium cation, [U V (η 8 -C 8 H 8 ) 2 ] + , and demonstrate using electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy and magnetometry that this formal U(V) complex has a 5 f 1 ground state. Enhanced uranium 5 f and 6 d mixing into filled δ-symmetry bonding orbitals in uranocenium, compared to uranocene, amplifies interorbital electron–electron repulsion, and counteracts bond length contraction, which minimises structural change. This manifests in solution where the uranocene/uranocenium redox couple exhibits near-ideal electrochemical reversibility, and in the solid-state where X-ray diffraction studies show minimal U–C bond length change upon oxidation. This demonstrates a case where actinide covalency governs molecular structure and physical properties across both solid and solution phases.

item.dc:creator: Yi-An Lai
Muxin Xiong
Jingwen Sun
Aijian Huang

Hongyuan Sheng
Jennifer Kim

item.description:
Authors: Yi-An Lai, Muxin Xiong, Jingwen Sun, Aijian Huang, Max Van Fleet, Hongyuan Sheng, Jennifer Kim, Felisha Kuo, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Autonomous experimentation offers a time-efficient route towards accelerated catalyst discovery, but current practices often rely on black-box models that are difficult to interpret. Here we demonstrate the paradigm of interpretable autonomous exploration of a 12-dimensional space in the electrocatalytic hydrogen evolution reaction by integrating an interpretable decision-making artificial intelligence with a fully automated electrochemical platform. Guided by a human’s chemistry-informed hypothesis, a chemistry-infused bandit is established to reflect the locally quadratic approximation between synthetic conditions and electrocatalytic activities near the explored optimum region. Not only does such a decision-making bandit lead to the discovery of previously unreported, earth-abundant electrocatalysts at least comparable to Pt-based ones, the bandit also reveals model-derived hypothesis for how synthetic conditions affect the electrocatalysts’ performance near the identified local optima as autonomous inquiry proceeds, which is otherwise untenable from black-box ones. Incorporating chemistry-informed hypothesis into the decision-making bandit is generally applicable to any chemistry problem and offers a framework for autonomous investigation, advancing hypothesis generation for catalyst’s design principles beyond simple optimization.

Authors: Xiaodi Shi, Laurent Oziel, Jonathan P. Benskin, Örjan Gustafsson, Anna Sobek
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11074
Abstract: Abstract Global oceans store large quantities of human-made persistent hydrophobic organic contaminants (HOCs), driven by the organic carbon (OC) cycle. Despite diverse organic matter composition, bulk OC is typically treated as a uniform sorbent when assessing HOC fate. Significant uncertainty remains regarding the factors controlling variability in the sorption of HOCs by organic matter. Using surface sediments across the Eurasian Arctic shelves, spanning a land-to-ocean continuum of OC, we show that polychlorinated biphenyl concentrations per unit marine‑derived OC are up to an order of magnitude higher than those per unit terrestrial OC. Coupling these empirical relationships with a state‑of‑the‑art ocean biogeochemistry model shows that climate‑driven increases in marine primary production in the Eurasian Arctic shelves lead to 1.3 times more HOC removal from the water column. These findings reveal that both OC quantity and quality control the sediment HOC sink and that climate‑induced shifts in OC cycles may restructure HOC fate in the Arctic Ocean.

item.description:
Authors: Aniol Santo-Angles, Jiarui Yang, Ying Zhou, Wing Kwan Hannah Chu, Grace W. Lindsay, Kartik K. Sreenivasan
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract The neural mechanisms of multiple-item working memory are not well understood. In the current study, we address two competing hypotheses about the neural basis of sequential working memory: neural subspaces versus neural sequences. Using broadband MEG data from human participants, we applied dimensionality reduction and multivariate decoding techniques to test whether a sequence of items is maintained through the reactivation of individual items in sequence (neural sequences) or by organizing them into distinct low-dimensional subspaces (neural subspaces). Our results revealed behaviorally relevant, low-dimensional neural subspaces that organized memory representations according to ordinal position in the sequence, supporting the neural subspaces hypothesis. In contrast, we found no evidence of sequential neural replay during the retention period, contrary to the neural sequences hypothesis. In this work, we show that sequential working memory is maintained through structured geometric organization in low-dimensional representational space, rather than through the sequential reactivation of individual items, thus clarifying the mechanisms of multi-item working memory.

Authors: Xiaoqi Jiang, Maoxiong Zhao, Shaohua Yang, Lan Lan, Chao Song, Fang Wu, Yang Bu
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract High-numerical-aperture extreme-ultraviolet flat optics are constrained by undersampling of steep edge phase gradients, which reduces phase fidelity and high-angle diffraction efficiency. Here, we introduce a momentum-relay architecture that partitions large wavevector deflections across two cascaded elements. A 4:1 demagnification platform operating at 532 nm synthesizes an effective numerical aperture of 0.80, producing a measured first-dark-ring radius of 413.2 nm and resolving ~555 nm image-plane features across a 100 μm-diameter field of view. We further translate the concept to 13.24 nm using a compact xenon laser-produced-plasma source. Two Fresnel zone plates, each with a numerical aperture of approximately 0.33, cooperatively synthesize an effective numerical aperture of approximately 0.53. Here, we show that cascaded momentum relay provides a compact route to high-numerical-aperture extreme-ultraviolet projection while relaxing the feature-size and spatial-sampling requirements imposed on each element.

Authors: Lan Jiang, Bintao Li, Liusheng Lei, Zishu Liu, Wei Sun, Liping Ma, Chang-Jun Cha, Timothy Johnson, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Livestock manure is a prominent One Health setting for antimicrobial resistance (AMR), yet the contribution of viruses to resistome assembly remains unresolved. Here we compile the Livestock Manure Virus Database (LMVD), a global catalog of 1,330,372 viral operational taxonomic units reconstructed from 4,017 metagenomes. Livestock manure viral communities exhibit restricted biogeographic distributions, and antibiotic use and farming scale show the highest relative predictive importance for viral diversity. Viral genomes contained 78 antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) subtypes, representing 9.1% of resistome diversity in livestock manure, but virus-encoded ARGs were infrequent. Bacteriophages instead showed extensive predicted links to bacterial hosts, with nearly all antibiotic-resistant bacteria linked to viruses, predominantly temperate viruses, and enrichment in pathogenic antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Together, these findings place bounds on the contribution of viruses to direct ARG dissemination and indicate that lysogenic interactions with resistant hosts may shape AMR risk.

Authors: Joseph Mallalieu, Jonathan L. Carrivick, Matthias Huss, Iestyn D. Barr, Nicholas E. Barrand, Cassandra L. Raby
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10873
Abstract: Abstract The environment in which a glacier terminates can strongly influence its behaviour, stability and future evolution, yet the relationship between terminus type and glacier dynamics at the global scale remains poorly constrained. Here we present a globally-complete classification of glacier termini distinguishing between land, lake, marine and shelf environments, and integrate it with datasets of glacier geometry, dynamics and climate. We show that although lake-, marine- and shelf-terminating glaciers comprise only 3.2% of glaciers globally, they account for over half of global glacier area and mass loss. We also show that lake- and marine-terminating glaciers flow, on average, 10% and 44% faster than land-terminating glaciers, respectively. Furthermore, specific (area-normalised) mass loss rates at lake-terminating glaciers are 57% greater than those at land- and marine-terminating glaciers. Our findings underscore the need for improved representation of non-land glacier termini in models of glacier evolution and sea-level rise, and suggest that distinguishing the environmental and geometric controls of termini on glacier dynamics remains an important challenge for future research.

Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Enterovirus D68 (EV-D68) is a common cause of mild respiratory illness in children but is also linked to acute flaccid myelitis (AFM), a rare and severe neurological condition which can result in permanent paralysis. Tracking EV-D68 transmission is difficult because symptoms overlap with other common childhood illnesses, making case reporting unreliable. As a result, the burden of EV-D68 transmission remains poorly understood, particularly prior to the first widely recognised outbreak in 2014. Phylodynamic approaches offer a powerful alternative to case-based surveillance, inferring epidemiological parameters directly from pathogen genetic sequences. Here we show, using a birth-death-sampling phylodynamic model applied to publicly available EV-D68 sequences from the 1990s to 2023 collected in Europe and North America, that seasonal EV-D68 transmission was well established long before the 2014 outbreak brought the virus to widespread attention. Furthermore, we show that AFM case burden is strongly associated with the transmission dynamics of a specific EV-D68 clade, clade B, an association not seen for clades A and D. These findings suggest that clade-specific biological differences drive AFM risk, with important implications for surveillance prioritisation and the timing of future burden of neurological disease.

Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10874
Abstract: Abstract Fast qubit control is essential for scalable quantum computing. However, the strong driving that is required can induce significant leakage from the computational subspace, particularly in weakly anharmonic qubits. We demonstrate single qubit gates with a total leakage error consistently below 2.0 × 10 −5 on a transmon qubit, and obtain fidelities above 99.98% at 6.8 ns pulse duration in both X and X /2 gates. This is achieved by removing direct transitions beyond nearest-neighbor levels using double recursive applications of Derivative Removal by Adiabatic Gate pulse shape. We also introduce the amplified leakage error sequence which can directly measure the leakage error down to 10 −6 . We test single qubit gates across a range of pulse durations using multiple benchmarking methods to reveal the error channels. The presented approach can be straightforwardly adapted by other platforms.

item.title: Signaling by RasG12V requires EGFR function in vivo to trigger full downstream pathway activation
item.dc:creator: Patricia Vega-Cuesta

Jose F. de Celis
item.description:
Authors: Patricia Vega-Cuesta, Ana López-Varea, Ana Ruiz-Gómez, Jose F. de Celis
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Ras proteins regulate signaling pathways initiated by tyrosine kinase receptors, and activating Ras mutations are drivers in cancer and RASophaties. The development of therapies against these diseases requires a profound understanding of how Ras mutations modify pathway output and interact with other pathway components. Here we generated G12V activating mutations in the Drosophila Ras1 locus and used Ras1 G12V and human KRASB G12V to analyze in vivo the consequences of endogenous Ras G12V expression and its interplay with other components of the EGFR/MAPK pathway. We find that Ras G12V acts as an amplifier of EGFR stimulation. Consistently, Ras G12V proteins respond to EGFR and can compensate for EGFR loss to generate basal levels of ERK activity. However, full pathway activation by Ras G12V is strictly dependent on EGFR function. Altogether, our results suggest that EGFR not only activates wild type Ras, but also Ras G12V , and support the notion that Ras G12V mutants are non-constitutively active.

item.title: Force-driven single-molecule transformations through tip-mediated stabilization of transition states

Authors: Kota Iwata, Ikutaro Hamada, Ranmaru Kuno, Taku Enomoto, Ryu Kuroki, Hidehiro Sakurai, Yoshiaki Sugimoto
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10868
Abstract: Abstract Mechanochemistry uses mechanical forces to drive chemical transformations, offering an energy-efficient alternative to traditional thermal, optical, or electrical reaction pathways. At the single-molecule scale, controlling structural changes with mechanical stimuli is fundamental for developing nanoscale devices and understanding chemical reactivity. In conventional single-molecule reactions driven by light or electrical currents, energy is supplied through one-way excitation processes, requiring the single-event energy input to exceed the activation energy barrier. Here we show that mechanically driven single-molecule reactions can bypass this limitation, proceeding with a net energy cost below the activation energy. By using atomic force microscopy to induce the structural inversion of individual, bowl-shaped sumanene molecules on a gold surface, we measure the mechanical energy spent during the transformation. The net energy cost is significantly lower than the theoretical activation energy. This sub-barrier reaction occurs because attractive van der Waals forces from the mesoscopic tip body stabilize the transition state more effectively than the final state. Our findings demonstrate a distinct energetic mechanism in mechanochemistry, highlighting alternative strategies for energy-efficient molecular manipulation.

Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11076
Abstract: Abstract Van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures allow the engineering of magnetic and electronic properties via interfacial orbital hybridization and charge transfer. The resulting electric fields can give rise to Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions, which may stabilize novel two-dimensional magnetic phases. Exploiting the inelastic phonon gap of graphene, scanning tunneling spectroscopy allows us to access the buried interface properties, and quantify Faraday-like screening. Our findings provide new insights and opportunities for electrically controlled interface magnetism, e.g. for spintronics and orbitronics devices.

Abstract: Abstract Gametogenesis rejuvenates the cellular lineage and excludes senescence-associated factors from gametes. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae , this involves sequestration of nuclear constituents into the Gametogenesis Uninherited Nuclear Compartment (GUNC), which is excluded from gametes. During meiosis II, Tom70 concentrates around the GUNC, where it recruits the nuclear envelope tethering protein Cnm1. Loss of CNM1 partially phenocopies tom70 ∆, consistent with parallel tethering interactions. These findings uncover a previously unrecognized organelle contact-dependent pathway that remodels the nuclear envelope to support selective nuclear inheritance. More broadly, they highlight how organelle contacts integrate with nuclear quality control to safeguard gamete integrity.

Abstract: Abstract Functional MRI (fMRI) has traditionally focused on grey matter activations, overlooking the contribution of white matter pathways to brain organisation. Yet evidence suggests that white matter constrains, modulates, and integrates signals across distant regions. Here, we introduce a framework to map the functional specialisation of white matter circuits using fMRI scans collected while participants watched naturalistic videos. An artificial intelligence framework applied to independent datasets confirmed the robustness and functional relevance of the identified parcels. This open-access framework also enables the interactive exploration of white matter functional organisation, offering a new lens on the neural bases of cognition.

Abstract: Abstract Natural disasters can spark demands for democratic accountability yet impose losses and displacement that depress participation. We study approximately 16,000 Swedish tourists exposed to the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami who returned home to intact communities. Unlike most people exposed to natural disasters, they faced no increase in the cost of voting, so the case is well suited to studying motivational responses to disaster exposure. We link a survivor registry to population-wide administrative data ( N up to 7 million) and use entropy balancing to compare survivors to matched non-exposed citizens over 25 years. Exposed individuals do not withdraw from participation. Their turnout is 1.4 percentage points higher in 2010 and 2018, a modest but persistent gap. The gap is more than twice as large among the bereaved. Mobilization is strongest among those exposed between ages 16 and 25, which is what habit formation would predict. A 2023 follow-up survey (3,956 respondents; N = 3198 to 3625 per analysis after item non-response) provides descriptive evidence that survivors still evaluate the government’s crisis response negatively and have shifted their partisan sympathies away from the then-incumbent party. The findings indicate that failed crisis management may have lasting consequences for turnout and potentially party choice, and that the electoral stakes of disaster response extend beyond the disaster zone.

Abstract: Abstract Gallstone disease is a highly prevalent and costly gastrointestinal disease. Yet, genetic variation in gallstone susceptibility and its implication in metabolic pathways remain to be explored. We report a trans-ancestry genome-wide association meta-analysis of gallstone disease including 100,856 cases and 1,596,602 controls in the UK Biobank, FinnGen, Biobank Japan, and Million Veteran Program. We identified 116 (59 novel) risk loci across meta-analysis and found replication in statistically compelling signals in the All of Us Research Program. A polygenic risk score constructed from trans-ancestry lead variants was positively associated with liver chemistry and alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency and negatively associated with total cholesterol and low-density lipoprotein levels among trans-ancestry and European ancestry groups in the Penn Medicine BioBank. Colocalization of risk loci with 44 traits and with expression quantitative trait loci from eight tissues yielded 321 and 110 significant colocalizations, respectively. These findings broaden our understanding of the genetic architecture of gallstone disease.

Authors: E. Mayner, Y. Zhumagulov, C. de Giorgio, F. Chu, P. P. Swain, G. E. Fantner, A. Kis, O. V. Yazyev, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Spin defects in two-dimensional materials are promising platforms for quantum information technologies and nanoscale sensing. The negatively charged boron vacancy ( $${\mathrm{V}}_{\mathrm{B}}^{-}$$ V B − ) in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is particularly attractive due to its sensitivity to temperature, magnetic fields, and pressure, but its application is limited by intrinsically weak photoluminescence (PL). Here we demonstrate a van der Waals heterostructure that enhances the PL intensity of $${\mathrm{V}}_{\mathrm{B}}^{-}$$ V B − by up to 45× at 4 Kelvin while preserving compatibility with ultrathin optoelectronic platforms. A quasi type-I band alignment at the PbI 2 –defected hBN interface facilitates efficient interlayer coupling to the defect, and strong spectral overlap supports fluorescence resonance energy transfer. Ab initio calculations indicate that this coupling enables a photon-ratcheting mechanism, in which optical absorption in PbI 2 generates a nonlinear polarization that drives $${\mathrm{V}}_{\mathrm{B}}^{-}$$ V B − excitation. This process is compatible with interlayer energy transfer while maintaining minimal electronic and spin hybridization and preserving optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) contrast. The heterostructure further exhibits improved sensitivity to external magnetic fields. These results establish a route for the enhancement of defect emission via interlayer optical coupling and introduce a general materials strategy for amplifying weak quantum defect signals in nanomaterials.

Abstract: Abstract Multi-Tb/s optical interconnects for artificial intelligence data centers necessitate high-speed, energy-efficient, and compact transceivers. However, conventional silicon Mach-Zehnder modulators are fundamentally limited by low modulation efficiency and large physical dimensions that typically extend several millimeters, requiring high-swing drivers and power-intensive digital signal processing to achieve data rates exceeding 100 Gb/s per lane. Here we show a silicon photonic crystal waveguide slow-light modulator that overcomes the bandwidth-efficiency trade-off via a built-in electro-optic equalizer. By monolithically integrating optical delay lines and crossings within segmented slow-light phase shifters, we synthesized an on-chip feedforward response that extends the 3-dB bandwidth. The fabricated modulator with a small device length of 320 µm demonstrated 140-Gb/s on-off keying operation with an energy consumption of 26 fJ/bit using drive voltages compatible with fin field-effect transistor-based complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor technology. Furthermore, four-level pulse amplitude modulation achieved 180 Gb/s without digital signal processing and 200 Gb/s with a low-complexity 11-tap digital equalizer. By reducing reliance on power-dissipating electronics, this strategy provides a potential route toward future dense multi-Tb/s co-packaged optics for energy-constrained switching systems.

Abstract: Abstract Insect-scale flapping-wing micro aerial vehicles offer substantial potential for applications such as search and rescue. However, stringent power and payload constraints at the sub-gram scale have precluded sustained untethered flight. Inspired by the high lift generated by full-circumferential rotor motion, this study presents a cross-shaped piezoelectric direct-drive V-wing structure. The structure uses a tuning-fork vibration mode to generate full-circumferential flapping, suppressing fuselage vibration without external anchoring and substantially improving the lift performance of the piezoelectric direct-drive flapping-wing micro aerial vehicle. Based on this principle, we developed a cross-shaped four-piezoelectric-actuator V-wing micro aerial vehicle weighing 389 mg with a wingspan of 6.8 cm, capable of generating a maximum lift of 1850 mg. Waveform modulation increases the efficiency of the 173 mg drive circuit to 45%, while mechanical self-stabilization suppresses attitude disturbances. Integrated with a 350 mg battery, the 984 mg system achieves untethered, sustained, stable flight for a sub-gram flapping-wing micro aerial vehicle. The maximum lift-to-weight ratio of the untethered flapping-wing micro aerial vehicle system is 1.88. Its maximum flight altitude exceeds 10 m, and its continuous flight duration under low-power operation exceeds 240 s. The system also demonstrates altitude-controlled and disturbance-resilient untethered flight.

Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Colloidal quantum dots (CQDs) short-wave infrared (SWIR) detectors (1-2 µm) are of great interest for a plethora of applications including autonomous driving, machine vision, night and adverse weather imaging, in view of their low-cost and compatibility to read-out electronics. However, to date, CQDs photodetectors still suffer from high dark current and thereby noise such that their performance remains inferior to epitaxially grown III-V semiconductors. This performance gap originates from the limited passivation of non-polar surfaces existent in large PbS CQDs needed to access the SWIR spectral range. Here we report on a lead-thiolate based chemistry that serves to passivate both polar and non-polar surfaces of PbS CQDs yielding inks with unprecedented optoelectronic quality evidenced by open circuit voltage deficit and dark current activation energies matching those of single crystalline semiconductors. As a result, we demonstrate infrared photodetectors with remarkable thermal resilience, very low dark current density ( ~ 34 nA cm −2 at −1 V) and a specific detectivity D* of ~8×10 12 Jones. The measured D* value is on par with that of commercially available InGaAs photodiodes (PDs).

item.title: NHEJ-mediated DNA synapsis and RPA-driven MRX exonuclease balance DNA end resection to control DSB repair

item.description:
Authors: Stefan Braunshier, Elda Cannavo, Vincent Morin, Sriram KK, Ananya Acharya, Giordano Reginato, Florian Morati, Virginie Ropars, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) are repaired by Ku-dependent non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) or DNA end resection-dependent homologous recombination (HR). Previously, it was shown that short-range resection by MRX-pSae2 can remove Ku from DSBs and initiate resection, showing flexibility in DSB repair pathway choice. However, which NHEJ intermediates can be disrupted by resection factors remains unknown. Using reconstituted reactions with purified S. cerevisiae proteins, we show here that short-range resection by MRX-pSae2 is not directly inhibited by any of the core NHEJ factors. Instead, we find that MRX-pSae2 is inhibited structurally. DNA synapsis, a dynamic NHEJ intermediate that bridges DSBs, strongly suppresses resection. Non-ligatable ends are refractory to MRX-pSae2 once synapsis formed, and NHEJ assemblies with catalytic mutants of DNA ligase IV that permit synapsis but do not allow ligation likewise inhibit resection. We further demonstrate that removal of Ku from DSBs requires RPA, which interacts with MRX and pSae2 to synergistically stimulate MRX 3′−5′ exonuclease activity, generating free 3′ overhangs. Our data support a model in which DNA synapsis temporarily prevents resection, allowing NHEJ to execute ligation. If ligation fails and synapsis dissociates, MRX-pSae2 and RPA promote resection that removes non-productive NHEJ assemblies and channels DSB repair toward HR. The data help explain the suppression of NHEJ by RPA observed in previous genetic experiments.

Abstract: Abstract While magnetometers based on nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond have emerged as the most important solid-state quantum sensors, ensembles are typically limited to a few percent optical contrast. This provides a perspective for highly sensitive magnetometry operated outside magnetically-shielded rooms for applications including magnetoencephalography, magnetic navigation, and magnetic anomaly detection.

Abstract: Abstract X-chromosome inactivation (XCI) is essential for extraembryonic tissue growth and embryo development in mice. However, species-specific differences in its timing and regulation have left its role in human development unclear. Furthermore, we show that XCI is needed for the survival of human female extraembryonic cells. Together, these findings link XCI to the formation of human extraembryonic lineages, with important implications for human reproductive biology.

item.dc:creator: Ashley J. Newton

Authors: Ashley J. Newton, Adefoluke E. Kuforiji, Philipp A. M. Schmidpeter
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Cell membranes are not only protective barriers but also active chemical environments that regulate protein structure and function. However, how individual lipid species influence membrane proteins across physiological concentration ranges, either as specific ligands or through bilayer-mediated solvent effects, remains poorly defined. Here, using the cyclic nucleotide-gated ion channel SthK reconstituted into defined membranes, we show that phosphatidic acid enhances channel activity across all tested concentrations but, at low mole fractions ( ~ 0.7-1 mol%), it selectively and cooperatively increases agonist potency, meeting criteria for a site‑specific allosteric ligand. In contrast, the zwitterionic lipid phosphatidylethanolamine modulates SthK activity exclusively through linear, solvent‑like effects across the same concentration range. Structural analysis reveals that low anionic lipid content expands the closed‑state conformational ensemble without promoting pore opening, providing a structural basis for lipid-dependent latent allostery. Together, these results establish lipid concentration as a governing regulatory variable that quantitatively distinguishes ligand‑like from solvent‑like mechanisms of membrane protein regulation.

Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10790
Abstract: Abstract Cell Painting is a popular high-content imaging assay that captures the shape and internal organization of 2D cell cultures at scale. While 3D cell cultures are more physiologically relevant models – especially for studying drug perturbations – they remain challenging to image because light scatters before it reaches the cultures’ interior. Here, we introduce a scalable method to adapt Cell Painting for 3D spheroids. We show that tissue-clearing, a technique that makes spheroids transparent, combined with a focusing routine that locates spheroids on the fly, enables Cell Painting at single-cell level inside intact spheroids. By profiling 52 clinically relevant drugs, we show that single-cell fingerprints clustered by biological pathway and resolved drug effects more robustly than those of flattened spheroid-wide views. Notably, the effect of two drugs, 5-fluorouracil and olaparib, nearly indistinguishable in 2D monolayers, diverged in spheroids. This finding was then corroborated by DNA-damage, cell-cycle, and gene-expression assays. The workflow runs on a spinning-disk confocal microscope in a standard 384-well plate format, making single-cell 3D profiling accessible to laboratories already performing Cell Painting.

Abstract: Abstract The transcription factor TFE3 coordinates cellular adaptation to stress. While its acute activation is cytoprotective, chronic TFE3 dysregulation is linked to diverse pathologies. Here, we characterize the cellular landscape of TFE3-NDD, a recently described neurodevelopmental disorder caused by mutations that disrupt the TFE3-Rag GTPase interface, leading to constitutive TFE3 nuclear localization. Using patient-derived fibroblasts, we show that TFE3-NDD is primarily a metabolic and homeostatic disorder. Mutant cells undergo a profound rewiring toward oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), resulting in metabolic rigidity and a vulnerability to energy failure. Despite a massive expansion of the lysosomal compartment, we observe a paradoxical qualitative failure characterized by impaired acidification, defective protease maturation, increased lysosomal exocytosis, and aberrant cathepsin K secretion. This secretory phenotype is coupled with a destabilized cell-extracellular matrix interface, marked by impaired migration, defective coordination between actomyosin tension and focal adhesion maturation, and a loss of synaptic stabilizers. Notably, TFE3-NDD shares a signature of high OXPHOS and ferroptosis resistance with TFE3-dependent cancers, such as translocation renal cell carcinoma. Our findings reveal how the chronic hyperactivation of a protective stress-response factor collapses cellular homeostasis, providing a mechanistic framework for the tissue malformations and neurodevelopmental deficits that define TFE3-NDD.

Abstract: Abstract The gut microbiome in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is enriched in proinflammatory bacteria, yet defining a consistent dysbiotic signature is challenging, due to substantial variation between individuals and over time. Finally, defining an inflammatory index, we demonstrated that inflammation explains much of the observed variation in microbial composition and abundance. Together, our findings indicate that inflammation associates and likely contributes to loss of commensals, thereby limiting microbiome recovery and resilience.

Abstract: Abstract Graphene nanoscrolls (GNSs), one-dimensional nanostructures formed by rolling up a single sheet of graphene, exhibit electronic and mechanical properties distinct from the original graphene sheet. The nanoscroll structure allows the intercalation of metal chloride molecules, resulting in an increase of the electrical conductivity. Furthermore, heteronanoscrolls of graphene and MoS 2 are realized by stretching MoS 2 /graphene heterostacks, exhibiting clear optical response. item.description:
Authors: Eugene Tan, Mauricio van den Berg, Adam Saddler, Camilo Vargas, Daniel J. Weiss, Amelia Bertozzi-Villa, Samir Bhatt, Tasmin L. Symons, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Since their rapid adoption from the mid 2000s, insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) have been one of the most impactful malaria interventions in Africa. Facing insecticide resistance and ever-increasing resource constraints, there is a growing need to revise previous modelling efforts of ITN coverage to better reflect the current epidemiological reality. Comprehensive estimates of ITN coverage must account for factors such as net type, net age, and user behaviours. By leveraging improved data availability, we propose a mathematically rigorous ITN coverage model that extends previous national-level models to the subnational level across 44 countries in Africa. The presented Multitype-ITN (MITN) model is used to construct longitudinal estimates of net demography by age and type from 2006-2024, and provide insights on potential sources of ITN distribution inefficiencies. Our findings show a significant increase in the uptake of next-generation ITNs, reflecting an increasingly diverse market. However, longitudinal trends suggests stagnation in key metrics of net coverage (nets-per-capita, access and use), alongside a downwards trend in utilisation – number of users per net, coupled with observed stationary use rates – proportion of people with access that also use nets. There are also early signs of interventions failing to meet the demands of increasing populations.
